notes.meaning: Jesus turned to speak to the crowds and to His followers. The religious leaders had just failed to trap Him with questions, so He now openly warned the people about their teachers.
The teachers of the law and Pharisees held the official role of explaining God's law. Sitting in Moses' seat meant they had the recognized authority to read and teach the Scriptures to the nation.

Jesus told the people to respect the law of Moses whenever these teachers correctly read and explained it. However, they were not to copy how the leaders lived, because the leaders did not practice what they preached.
The religious leaders piled heavy rules and human traditions onto the people, demanding strict obedience. Yet they offered no help or mercy to anyone struggling under that weight.

Everything the leaders did was designed to win public praise and look holy to other people. They wore extra-wide prayer boxes containing Scripture passages and lengthened the tassels on their clothes to draw attention to their religious habits.
These leaders loved being treated as important guests at big dinners. In the synagogues, they sought out the front seats that faced the congregation so everyone would notice them.
They enjoyed receiving respectful public greetings in crowded markets. They also loved being addressed with the title Rabbi, which honored them as great and learned masters of the law.
Jesus told His followers not to seek honorable titles like Rabbi for themselves. The Messiah is their only true Teacher, and all believers stand on equal ground as brothers and sisters.
Followers of Jesus must not give any human leader the absolute spiritual authority that belongs only to God. Believers have one true Father in heaven who rules over their lives and consciences.

differ.view: God alone possesses supreme fatherly authority over the soul, though earthly fathers may still be given rightful honor without raising ministers to Christ's place.
Believers must reject any title that claims lordly power over the conscience, while natural parents and spiritual guides may still be loved and respected.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: This command condemns using titles with prideful independence from God, while calling priests spiritual fathers reflects their pastoral care under God's fatherhood.

notes.meaning: Jesus repeated that His disciples should not be called masters or directors of other people's faith. Only Christ has the right to lead, guide, and instruct His church.
In God's kingdom, true greatness is not measured by rank or having people wait on you. The greatest person among the disciples is the one who willingly serves everyone else.
God will bring down anyone who tries to lift themselves up in pride. At the same time, He will honor and lift up the person who chooses a humble and lowly place.

Jesus declared sorrow and judgment on the religious leaders for their hypocrisy, which means acting a part while hearts remain far from God. By rejecting Jesus and teaching human rules, they refused to enter God's kingdom and kept others from entering as well.

The leaders took advantage of vulnerable widows, using religion to get hold of their property. To cover up this greed, they offered lengthy public prayers, which only ensured a harsher judgment for their deceit.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note this verse is absent from the oldest Greek manuscripts and was likely added here from parallel passages in Mark and Luke.

notes.meaning: The Pharisees traveled far and wide to convert a single person to their religious sect. Yet once they gained that convert, they taught him their own legalistic habits, making him twice as hardened in sin as they were.

Jesus called these teachers blind guides because they created foolish loopholes for keeping promises. They claimed that swearing by the temple was not binding, but swearing by the gold in the temple forced a person to keep the oath.
Jesus exposed their foolish thinking by asking whether the gold was greater than the temple. The gold had no special holiness on its own, but was made sacred only because it belonged to God's house.
The scribes also made up rules about the altar of sacrifice. They taught that swearing by the altar meant nothing, but swearing by the gift on the altar created an unbreakable promise.
Jesus pointed out that an offering on the altar has no holiness by itself. It is the altar dedicated to God that makes the gift holy and acceptable.
Swearing an oath by the altar includes everything placed upon it. Anyone making such a pledge is appealing to the holy place of sacrifice and to God Himself.
When a person swears by the temple, that oath cannot be treated lightly. It directly involves God, who chose the temple as His dwelling place among His people.
Anyone who swears by heaven is really swearing by God's throne. Every oath ultimately appeals to the living God who sits on that throne and judges truthfulness.

The leaders were remarkably careful to give a tithe, or tenth part, of even tiny garden herbs like mint, dill, and cumin. Yet they ignored far more important commands of God, such as doing justice, showing mercy, and remaining faithful.

Jesus used wordplay to show how backward their priorities were. They carefully strained their drink through cloth so they would not swallow a tiny unclean gnat, yet they swallowed an entire unclean camel without noticing.

The Pharisees washed the outside of dishes very thoroughly according to ceremonial rules. Inside, however, their lives and tables were filled with wealth stolen from others and spent on selfish pleasures.
Jesus told them to start by cleaning the inside of the cup. When a person's heart and desires are made pure and honest, their outward actions will naturally become truly clean as well.

Tombs were coated with white lime each spring so travelers could clearly see them and avoid touching them. They looked bright and clean on the outside, but inside they held decaying bones and corruption.
In the very same way, these leaders appeared deeply religious and moral to everyone watching them. Beneath the surface, their hearts were packed with pretending and open disregard for God's law.
The scribes and Pharisees spent money building tombs and decorating monuments for God's ancient prophets. They wanted everyone to think they deeply honored those holy men of old.

They claimed that if they had lived centuries earlier, they would never have joined their ancestors in killing God's messengers. They believed they were far too righteous to commit such terrible sins.

By speaking of those murderers as their fathers, they acknowledged their family heritage. More than that, their hatred toward Jesus proved they shared the very same murderous spirit as their ancestors.
Jesus told them to go ahead and finish what their ancestors had started. He knew they were about to complete the nation's rebellion by plotting His own death.

Jesus called them a family of poisonous snakes, echoing the sharp warning John the Baptist had given years earlier. Because they clung so stubbornly to their sins, they could not escape God's final judgment in hell.

Jesus announced that He would send them Christian apostles, teachers, and messengers of the gospel. Instead of welcoming them, these leaders would beat them in synagogues, chase them from city to city, and kill them.

Because this generation repeated and completed all the sins of the past, it would face the judgment due for every righteous person murdered in Old Testament history. That line of martyrs stretched from Abel in Genesis all the way to Zechariah at the end of the Hebrew Scriptures.
Jesus solemnly promised that this awful judgment would fall upon the people then living. This warning came to pass when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and its temple about forty years later.

Jesus cried out over Jerusalem with deep sorrow, mourning how the city had killed God's prophets through the ages. He had longed to shelter her people with the tender care of a mother hen protecting her chicks, but they refused His love.

differ.view: This refers to Christ's outward call through preaching, which sinful people freely refuse, while those God purposed to save are drawn irresistibly by His Spirit.
Christ genuinely yearned to gather the people across history, showing that sinners alone bear the blame when they perish through their own willful unbelief.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Christ as God truly willed to gather all of Jerusalem, showing that human free will has the power to resist divine grace.

notes.meaning: Jesus declared that their temple was now abandoned and left empty. Because God was departing from it, the sacred building was handed over to ruin.

Jesus announced that the nation would not see Him again until they were ready to welcome Him as the blessed Messiah sent by the Lord. This looked forward to a future day when Israel would turn to Him in repentance and faith.
